verdict.root_cause: All sampled failing PlaceOrder traces break at one hop: checkoutservice's client span for ShippingService/GetQuote inside prepareOrderItemsAndShippingQuoteFromCart returns an error fast (~2.6-3.8ms), aborting the order before payment. Cart, product-catalog and currency calls all succeed in the same traces, and checkout's own self-time is negligible, so checkoutservice is only propagating. The shipping/quote path is the failing mechanism; quoteservice alerting alongside the dependent services at 01:58:15 fits a quote-side fault. No change record exists for checkoutservice, cartservice or productcatalogservice, and no change query was run against shippingservice/quoteservice, so the triggering act is unidentified. Class is best read as a fast dependency-side error return from the shipping quote path rather than exhaustion or a bad checkout artifact.
verdict.reasoning: Traces [tr_49540b038abd] localise the fault deterministically to GetQuote and clear cart, catalog, currency and payment. Logs [tr_12b0de494d5b] corroborate: intake lines continue but payment/email/message-write follow-ups stop after ~01:56, i.e. orders abort before payment, matching the trace shape. Metrics [tr_d7d7a1edba4f] show sustained ~22% checkout errors, partial not total, consistent with a deterministic failure on one branch of traffic. Change logs [tr_fbdbde8d8e3d] rule out a checkout deploy/config/flag; cartservice logs [tr_a184e8302966] show no backing-store errors. Fault class is left unknown because the shipping server span completes without error while the caller span errors, and no shippingservice/quoteservice logs, metrics or change history were gathered to say whether the mechanism is a bad quote artifact, a wrong endpoint value, or resource pressure.
open_questions: Why does the shippingservice server span complete clean while checkout's client span errors - a status mapping issue, a non-2xx quote response, or a transport/deadline mismatch?
No dispatch touched shippingservice or quoteservice logs, metrics, or change history; the actual failing mechanism and any upstream change there are unobserved.
What happened between 01:44 and 01:56 in checkout logs - truncation dropped the 01:55 onset entirely, so the error text at first failure is unknown.
Why do ~78% of checkout calls still succeed - is the failure keyed to particular carts/items/currencies?

alternatives.root_cause: quoteservice (the HTTP quote backend behind shippingservice) began returning error responses that shippingservice forwards to checkout.
alternatives.why_not: quoteservice alerted at 01:58:15, but traces show shipping's downstream HTTP client span completing without error, so the error appears to originate at or above shipping rather than in the quote backend.

alternatives.root_cause: checkoutservice itself mishandles the GetQuote response (client-side deadline, deserialisation, or validation) and marks an otherwise valid reply as an error.
alternatives.why_not: No checkoutservice change of any kind is recorded [tr_fbdbde8d8e3d] and its self-time is ~0.1ms, so a spontaneous client-side regression with no deploy is less likely than a dependency-side change.

proposal.expected_effect: No action is taken, so nothing should change: checkoutservice's error ratio should remain near its observed 0.22 mean (sum by(service_name)(rate(calls_total{service_name="checkoutservice",status_code="STATUS_CODE_ERROR"}[2m])) / total), PlaceOrder traces should keep erroring at the checkoutservice client span for ShippingService/GetQuote, and checkout logs should keep showing PlaceOrder intake lines with no payment/email/message-write follow-up. The next observable step is diagnostic, not remedial: a change_history query scoped to shippingservice and quoteservice, and a severity-filtered log query on checkout-service for 01:50-01:56, which would either name a change to revert or name the error text at onset. Until one of those returns something, no permitted action has a target.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if a change_history query on quoteservice or shippingservice returns a deploy, image change, or config edit inside the incident window — that would meet rollback_image's or revert_config's preconditions and give a concrete target on the failing path. It is also wrong if the checkout error ratio keeps climbing past ~0.275 toward total failure while we wait, which would make the cost of inaction exceed the cost of a speculative restart. Note that neither restart nor rollback of checkoutservice would be visible as a fix here anyway: the erroring hop is checkout's client span for a call whose server side completes clean, so recreating checkout's container would not change the quote-side return.
proposal.risk: The risk of abstaining is elapsed time: roughly 22% of checkout calls continue to fail and no order reaches payment, so revenue loss accrues for as long as the quote path is unexamined. The risk I am avoiding is larger and specific — every permitted action here would have to target a service the evidence has already cleared. rollback_image on checkoutservice has no recorded prior tag (change history is empty for it) and would be a no-op deploy that resets live connections; restart_service on checkoutservice would discard cache and drop in-flight orders on a process the logs show is alive and serving steadily, addressing no named mechanism; either would also muddy the timeline for whoever investigates quoteservice next, since a container recreate is itself a change that later queries will surface.
proposal.blast_radius: No service is touched, so no caller sees a connection reset. The ongoing failure continues to be visible to frontend (which fronts the erroring PlaceOrder path) and to the alerted accountingservice, emailservice and frauddetectionservice downstream of uncompleted orders; shippingservice and quoteservice remain unobserved. Had I proposed a checkoutservice action instead, frontend would have seen the reset directly and all order-completion consumers would have seen a further gap.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical multi-service failure starting at checkout with four downstream consumers alerting minutes later; nothing here can be dismissed and no open incident exists to fold it into. The fan-out pattern is consistent with a checkout-side fault but the alerts alone don't indicate which class.
